In the UK, Rape Crisis offers support on 0808 500 2222 in England and Wales, 0808 801 0302 in Scotland, or 0800 0246 991 in Northern Ireland. In the US, Rainn offers support on 800-656-4673. In Australia, support is available at 1800Respect (1800 737 732). Other international helplines can be found at ibiblio.org/rcip/internl.html

articles.title: All hostages rescued after Colombian security forces storm supermarket, says president
articles.summary: Operation in which one hostage-taker was killed ends daylong siege in Cartagena shopping centre, where 30 people were initially held
body: Colombian police have stormed a supermarket in one of the country’s most popular tourist cities, ending a daylong siege in which all the hostages were freed and one hostage-taker was killed.

Abelardo de la Espriella, the far-right president, travelled to the Caribbean port city of Cartagena to follow the final hours of negotiations and the tactical assault, in which special forces officers broke through blocked entrances and detonated stun grenades.

When masked and armed assailants stormed the supermarket at about 8.30am on Tuesday local time, 30 people including customers and employees were taken hostage, many of whom could be seen through windows with their hands and feet tied. Ten had already been released over the course of the day.
When, after 17 hours in captivity, the final 20 people were freed at about 1.30am on Wednesday, four of the hostage-takers were arrested and one was killed.

In a video posted outside the supermarket – about 6 miles from the old city and its 500-year-old fortress walls, which are visited by thousands of tourists every year – De la Espriella celebrated the end of the operation.

“One of the criminals was killed. They were given the opportunity to surrender and release the hostages; they rejected that opportunity and we acted forcefully,” he said. He appeared with a gun on his waist, as he has on several other occasions in public as part of his populist security rhetoric.
Related: Colombia’s president arrives at scene of supermarket hostage siege in tourist city

The president arrived in Cartagena late on Tuesday afternoon from Villavicencio, about 684 miles inland, where he had been dealing with the aftermath of another attack on Monday night, when a car bomb was detonated outside the headquarters of the Meta departmental government.
More than 20 people were injured and a security guard was killed, and the president attributed the attack to a dissident faction of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc).

De la Espriella, however, denied that the supermarket hostage-taking had been carried out by a “terrorist group”, as he describes the groups involved in Colombia’s decades-long armed conflict, saying instead that those responsible were common criminals.
The president said they had tried to rob an armoured cash-in-transit vehicle but, after being spotted by private security – who then alerted police – they took refuge in the supermarket.

Commenting on what he called an “extraordinary” rescue operation, De la Espriella said his government was acting out of “the need to defend our people and go after all the criminals with an iron fist”.
The daylong hostage siege took place on a symbolic day for security in Colombia: the 10th anniversary of the country’s landmark peace accord with Farc guerrillas.

In office for just over three months, the president – previously a lawyer and businessman – is a fierce critic of the peace deal and has focused his government on returning to a strategy of full-on confrontation with criminal groups, breaking completely with the “total peace” plan of his predecessor, the leftist Gustavo Petro.

Although some indicators show slight improvements in areas such as homicides and kidnappings, recent days have been marked by a strong response from criminal groups: in addition to the car bombing, another guerrilla group carried out the first-ever drone attack on a departmental capital on Monday.
On Tuesday night, five departments were left without electricity, and De la Espriella said criminals used explosives to bring down power pylons.
“These criminal acts constitute the response of terrorist groups to the forceful offensive being carried out by the national government to restore order and security across the country,” he said.

articles.title: Spain has been hit hard by the climate crisis. Why are politicians saying so little about it before the election?
articles.summary: Wildfires and floods can do little to move climate change up voters’ list of priorities, experts say
body: Beneath the blackened branches of a pine tree that rises high above a landscape of scorched hillsides and the odd charred and ruined house, two older men address the obvious. Four months after one of the summer’s many wildfires threatened to devour the hamlet of El Morro, an hour west of Madrid, local people are still counting the cost and awaiting compensation.

“Look at that house,” said Esteban Pérez, pointing to one of the properties that did not make it through July’s flames. “Everything inside is scorched, completely destroyed. You can still see the windows, but they’re gutted. The entire structure of the house next to mine had to be torn down, too. And they’ve given the owner nothing so far.”
His friend nods and offers a more laconic observation: “We’re still screwed here.”

And yet, for all the abundant recent evidence of the effects of the climate crisis around Spain’s capital and in the eastern region of Valencia, which is still recovering from the deadly floods that killed more than 230 people two years ago, there has been little mention of the issue as the country prepares for this week’s snap general election.
Pérez is not surprised that the politicians are keener to focus on housing and immigration than on Spain’s immense vulnerability to climatic disasters and the attendant costs.
“The thing is, they only talk about whatever interests them during the campaign,” he said. “If something doesn’t interest them, they don’t talk about it.”

Four hundred kilometres to the east in the Valencian municipality of Benetússer, Rut Moyano, a member of the local emergency and reconstruction committee, has been stunned by the lack of focus on the climate crisis.

“It’s not just the floods we have experienced, there are also the forest fires; the temperatures the Mediterranean is reaching; the fact that we spend our summers in a state of permanent heatwave, and the droughts,” she said.

“Everything is changing because of these factors, but it’s as if there’s an attempt – I don’t know if it’s an intentional silencing – but certainly a failure to give the issue the importance it truly deserves.”
Despite the lack of stump speeches and calls to action, climate policies do feature in this year’s manifestos.

The ruling socialist party – which describes the climate emergency as “one of the greatest challenges of our time” – has promised to “speed up a just ecological transition, boost renewable energy, move towards greater energy autonomy, and turn sustainability into a source of employment, innovation and prosperity”.
The conservative People’s party (PP) has vowed to “act from science and without dogmatism” when it comes to fighting climate change and pursuing decarbonisation.

Meanwhile the far-right Vox party, which could well form a coalition with the PP, has pledged to tackle “climate fanaticism” and to put an end to international agreements that “hinder our productive development and the prosperity of Spanish workers, families, businesses and industries”.

Even though Spain’s three biggest parties enthusiastically defend their very different climate policies on paper, some observers are unsurprised at their reluctance to place them centre-stage at rallies and in interviews.

Jordi Muñoz, an associate professor of political science at the University of Barcelona, is part of a team that has researched the effect that natural disasters, such as the Valencia floods, have on voter behaviour.

“Our research reveals that the 2024 floods significantly increased the perception among Valencians that their region is particularly affected by climate change,” he said. “However … this did not translate into greater concern about climate change relative to other issues, nor did it increase the likelihood of people identifying climate change as one of the country’s top three problems.
“Furthermore, we observed no increase in support for climate policies, nor any rise in individual actions taken to mitigate climate change.”
Given the lack of votes to be had on the issue, Muñoz added, it’s hardly unexpected that parties opt to “pay it no attention during the campaign”.

Nuria Blázquez, a spokesperson for Ecologists in Action, acknowledges that the sheer scale and effects of the climate crisis are a tough sell. Even after the fires, floods, heatwaves and droughts of recent years, both politicians and voters tend to focus on specific failings in disaster response rather than the over-arching cause.

“In the case of the Valencia floods, the discussion was centred on whether the proper alerts were sent,” she said. “With the wildfires, the focus shifts to a lack of vegetation clearing or similar factors – problems that are somewhat easier to address.

“Climate change feels a bit more abstract; it’s clearly a problem, but it’s so difficult to tackle that the general public finds it much easier to look for a culprit in simpler, more tangible things.”

But Blázquez also warned that a huge amount is at stake as Spain prepares to vote – and that the results of the election will be felt well beyond the country’s borders. Under the leadership of the prime minister Pedro Sánchez – and his former environment minister Teresa Ribera, who now serves as the EU’s green transition chief – Spain has become what she terms the bloc’s “leader in environmental and climate policy”.
But Sunday’s election could change all that.

“Neither the PP – and especially not Vox – seem to acknowledge the reality of the situation. In fact, Vox’s narrative suggests that climate change basically doesn’t exist,” added Blázquez. “So we have no reason to be hopeful about a potential PP-Vox government … Without a doubt, that’s where the biggest loss would be: the total disappearance of any hope for leadership on environmental and climate issues within the EU.”

articles.title: UK embassy in Japan warns of rise in drink spiking and credit card fraud at Tokyo bars
articles.summary: Social media campaign fronted by British rapper Shao Dow advises tourists not to let their guard down
body: The British embassy in Tokyo has launched a social media campaign warning visitors to exercise caution after a rise in cases of drink-spiking and credit card fraud against tourists in the Japanese capital.

In a recent clip made in conjunction with the embassy, the British rapper and manga artist Shao Dow, a frequent visitor to Japan, notes that although the country “is incredibly safe, that doesn’t mean you can let your guard down”.

He warns that young male tourists are particularly susceptible to being lured into bars on the promise of being able to chat to attractive, English-speaking women. They are then served drug-laced drinks and enormous sums are charged to their credit cards.
Drink-spiking cases involving British and other international tourists have been on the rise in the past two years in popular nightlife districts such as Roppongi, Shibuya and Kabukicho.

Some victims have lost up to £30,000 (US$39,000) in a single night, Dow says, and wake up with no memory of what happened. “Look, do me a favour,” he adds, “Stay alert, trust your gut, keep an eye on your stuff and don’t follow strangers into bars.”

Police in Tokyo have come under pressure to tackle the rise in incidents targeting tourists. Earlier this month, 160 riot police conducted predawn raids on two establishments in Kabukicho after reports they had ripped off customers. Five people were arrested.

Between January and October, police recorded 340 cases – up 195 from last year – in the Shinjuku area after customers, some of whom were lured into bars by street touts, were charged extortionate sums. In one case, ¥9.6m ($60,000) was allegedly charged to a customer’s credit card.

According to the newspaper Asahi Shimbun, victims have paid ¥390m in total and foreign nationals had been the targets in 70% of cases. The newspaper quoted a senior investigator as saying the reported crimes were the “tip of the iceberg” since many visitors returned home before they realised they had been swindled, while others had left Japan without reporting the incidents to police.
Reports say the rise in cases was being fuelled by Japan’s tourism boom. A record 42.7 million people visited Japan last year, including 530,000 from the UK.
The Guardian has approached the Japan National Tourism Organisation for comment.

articles.title: General Synod could vote to ban C of E clergy from supporting Restore Britain
articles.summary: Exclusive: Private members’ motion comes amid concern about Christian symbols being appropriated by the far right
body: Church of England clergy could be banned from joining or supporting the hard-right Restore Britain party under a motion put forward for debate at the General Synod.

The move is an attempt to replicate the decision by bishops 17 years ago prohibiting clergy from belonging to or supporting the British National party, declaring its policies incompatible with church teaching on racial equality.

It comes against a backdrop of concerns about Christianity and Christian symbols being appropriated by the far right, including the anti-Muslim activist Tommy Robinson, and support for him from some pastors.

A vicar from a historic west London parish is among those fronting a “carol concert” next month organised by Robinson, who is expected to be jailed days later after his conviction for harassing two journalists.

Those behind the Church of England private members’ motion on Restore Britain membership are gathering signatures. It could be debated next year if 100 are collected, and would be expected to pass with support from many in the synod’s largest bloc of members, the liberal-leaning Together for the Church of England network, and others including some in the Evangelical Group.

Rupert Lowe, the leader of Restore Britain, described the motion as “outrageous”. “We will fight them in the court,” said the Great Yarmouth MP, who formed the party after falling out with Nigel Farage and leaving Reform UK. “I am not tolerating it.”

Sam Wilson, a lay member of the synod and youth worker in Altrincham, Greater Manchester, said he had proposed the motion after witnessing what he described as an upsurge in far-right activity on the streets and racialised language online.

Restore has been polling at as much as 5% and has become a magnet for far-right activists, including some who have explicitly drawn a link between Christianity and British identity. Members include Calvin Robinson, a cleric and former GB News presenter who was pictured along with Lowe at a Restore Britain event in London this month and is facing calls for his deportation from the US after saying Jews should be “driven out of America”.

Wilson told the Guardian: “My motivation is not that there is a large number of vicars who are supportive of Restore, but more that I think it is incumbent on the church to really establish a position and draw a line in terms of what is acceptable and not acceptable debate.”

The motion states that the synod, the national governing and legislative assembly of the church, affirms that “all people are created in the image of God and that racism is a sin”. It calls on bishops to exercise their power under section 3(3) of the Clergy Conduct Measure 2026 to make a declaration that the policies, objectives, activities and public statements of Restore Britain are incompatible with the Church of England’s teaching on the equality of persons or groups of different races. Section 3(3) allows for clergy to be suspended and ultimately defrocked.

Wilson added: “The last time anything like this was debated was in relation to the BNP and it passed with near unanimity, so there is confidence that this will also pass. A fear back then was that the church debating these parties could give them undue oxygen and publicity but that has changed now with X and other platforms.”

Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, has increasingly made Christian nationalist rhetoric part of his brand and is planning a “carol service” in central London on 12 December. It will be addressed by a range of far-right supporters. Those billed to speak include Father Luke Dobson, a Church of England priest and vicar of St George’s Headstone in Harrow, London.

Dobson has previously appeared alongside far-right activists, including members of Restore Britain, where he has said that deportations are about “maintaining our Christian culture”. At other times he has spoken of the need for the Church of England to rediscover “the lost art of excommunication” and apply it to those who refused to renounce “deceptive doctrines” in order for the church to be “spotless and pure”.

He also said that issues such as abortion and immigration were interconnected, adding that immigrants would not be needed if abortion was not allowed. “Immigration brings a degradation to our culture as English because other cultures are coming in who are not in a Christian mindset or culture,” he added.

articles.title: Indian Cockroach movement leader asks court for permission to fly to UK
articles.summary: Officials at Delhi airport stopped Saurav Das from boarding flight to Britain, where students have invited him to speak
body: A leader of India’s youth-led Cockroach movement has asked the Delhi high court to give him permission to fly to the UK after immigration officials at Delhi airport stopped him boarding a flight early on Tuesday morning.

The court is scheduled to hear Saurav Das’s case on Thursday morning. His lawyer asked the court for a quick hearing because Das has by now already missed some of his engagements at British universities and can only attend the other events on his itinerary if he is allowed to fly out as soon as possible.
Das, 27, is one of the main faces of the Cockroach movement, which shot into the political firmament out of nowhere in May to challenge the Narendra Modi government with street protests.
The movement succeeded in forcing the education minister to resign in July over exam leaks and has since functioned as a pressure group.
Das had been invited by the Oxford Union Society to participate in a “fireside chat” on the movement.
Indian student groups at Edinburgh, Cambridge, Queen Mary University of London and the London School of Economics have also invited him to speak.
“Students want to know how we succeeded without any violence, how we began and where we are going. There is a great curiosity about the movement,” Das told the Guardian.
Reports in the Indian media have alleged that Das was informed well before the flight that his passport contained discrepancies.

“None of these reports is true,” said Das. “I received an email five hours before my flight saying that I should not use my passport for travel. It gave no reason. And I did not see the email until I arrived at Delhi airport. What’s more, I’ve travelled abroad before on this passport since it was issued in 2019 so what’s the problem with it now?”

He suspects that the government is using a frivolous case filed in Chennai against him as a pretext. The case has been filed, Das surmises, by someone hostile to the Cockroach movement and disputes his citizenship.

Das believes he was deliberately stopped by a government that is “scared” of someone such as him speaking abroad about the ideals of Mahatma Gandhi and Jawaharlal Nehru (independent India’s first prime minister) and that it wanted to make an example of him.
“It’s a chilling signal to young Indians that we can do what we like, that if we can do this to a leader of a movement, we can do this to you too,” said Das.
Related: After 80 years in Oxford, Naga ancestors are finally going home
In recent years, the government has stopped foreign speakers and academics, including several from the UK, from entering India.

Last year, Francesca Orsini, a professor at Soas University of London, was stopped at Delhi airport and deported despite holding a valid visa. The government said she had been blacklisted for allegedly conducting research and speaking at events while visiting on a tourist visa in 2024.
Also last year, Nitasha Kaul, a professor at Westminster University, was detained at Bangalore airport and deported for “anti-India activities”.

Some people who find themselves blacklisted have chosen to fight back. In 2023, the UK-based journalist Amrit Wilson had her overseas citizen of India card which allows free movement into India cancelled, also for alleged “anti-India activities”.
She took legal action and earlier this week, the Delhi high court ruled that the government had failed to give any concrete details of what it meant by “anti-India activities”.
The court has given the government a week to issue a fresh notice, this time giving specific reasons.

articles.title: China misusing Interpol to target dissidents, says leading UK lawyer
articles.summary: Concerns over Beijing’s use of ‘red notices’ as Hong Kong prepares to host police organisation’s general assembly
body: China is misusing Interpol to target and silence dissidents, a leading British lawyer has claimed, as Hong Kong prepares to host the police organisation’s general assembly for the first time.

Ben Keith, a specialist in “red notices” - the Interpol system under which national authorities are requested to locate and detain suspects - said he was working on five cases involving China making questionable requests through Interpol.

He revealed that he had also contacted officials at the law enforcement organisation in July on behalf of a group of five high-profile UK-based Chinese dissidents to find out if Beijing had sought the issuance of red notices relating to them.

Interpol responded in October that they were looking into his request for information but there had been no substantive information shared, he added, raising concerns that there might be data relating to the individuals on the Interpol system.

He said: “If there’s no data, than they will tell me there’s no data. If there is data, then they have to get permission from Hong Kong to tell me. It has been sometime now. Given the profile of these individuals, I think they may have had some data on them. That’s the fear.”

Many Hong Kong democracy campaigners who fled to the UK in recent years have British national (overseas) status but this does not protect them from red notices outside the UK and potential extradition to China.

A red notice is a request to law enforcement worldwide to locate and provisionally arrest a person pending extradition, surrender, or similar legal action. It is based on an arrest warrant or court order issued by the judicial authorities in the requesting country. Member countries apply their own laws in deciding whether to arrest a person.

Keith said: “The Russian playbook was to accuse political opponents or business opponents of some sort of really technical criminal offence of fraud, employment law breach, regulatory offence, that sort of thing, to disguise the real purpose of the request. The Chinese have taken that on.”

Hong Kong will host the 94th Interpol general assembly between 30 November and 3 December, attracting police chiefs from its 196 member countries to set global policing policy, approve budgets and activities, and pass binding resolutions.

Keith said that hosting the assembly offered an opportunity for China to “reputation wash”, arguing that Beijing ran a sophisticated public relations machine to hide the high proportion of red notice and extradition requests that were politically motivated.

The red notice system is used by China to target those sought under the state campaigns launched under President Xi Jinping to track down fugitives overseas and recover illicit funds, known as Operations Fox Hunt and Sky Net, it is claimed.

A new report, The Red Notice Trap, by Ben Keith and Rhys Davies of the legal firm IHR Advisors, draws on court judgments, Interpol records and Chinese-language official documents, to show how red notices fit into Beijing’s campaign to silence critics and bring them home for persecution.

It notes under a 2025 revision of the implementing regulations for the People’s Repubilc of China’s supervision law that red notice requests sit with extradition, judicial assistance, law enforcement cooperation, prosecution abroad, asset seizure and ‘ideological education’, as tools for the recovery of people.

Among the cases cited in the IHR Advisors report is that of Yidiresi Aishan – a Uyghur activist who is also known as Idris Hassan – who was arrested in July 2021, when arriving at Casablanca airport on a flight from Turkey, where he had been living.

He was detained on the basis of a red notice issued by Interpol at China’s request “for belonging to a terrorist organisation”. Within two weeks, Interpol suspended the notice as it breached its rules and it was later cancelled.
The Moroccan extradition proceedings carried on regardless and in December 2021 the country’s court of cassation approved Hasan’s surrender to China.

The UN committee against torture found that Hasan’s extradition would breach article 3 of the convention against torture and Morocco did not carry out the extradition But Hasan remained in detention until 12 February 2025 after spending nearly four years in prison on the basis of an Interpol red notice.
“His case shows the central weakness this report returns to: Interpol can correct its own data, but it cannot undo what national authorities have already set in motion”, the authors write.
Hasan, who now lives in Canada, said he no longer travelled and that his life had been thrown “upside down”.
“Four years of life have gone, just spent in prison, I could not be with my children,” he told the Guardian. “Everything has changed. I cannot describe this. But I trust Canada.”
Hasan added: “I don’t understand how this kind of the big organisation like Interpol how they took my name down without evidence, without nothing. Just put my name out.”
Interpol and the Chinese embassy have been approached for comment.

articles.title: Wednesday briefing: Who will be the United Nations’ next leader – and what is at stake?
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: The UN secretary-general is one of the highest-profile diplomatic gigs on the planet. A look at how they are chosen – and how much power the new one will have
body: Good morning. How many former UK prime ministers can you name? What about US presidents? Now, try to reel off a list of United Nations secretary-generals.
Congratulations if you listed more than four (there are nine in total). Few friends I quizzed got beyond António Guterres, Ban Ki-moon and Kofi Annan, or an occasional Boutros Boutros-Ghali.

If you scored poorly, best swot up: the UN sec-gen is the most high-profile, influential diplomatic gig on the planet, and soon we’ll have a new one. After 10 years in the top job, incumbent António Guterres is bowing out, and the race to succeed him is hotting up. Early next week, a key vote will reveal if any of the frontrunners can garner the support needed.
But how are they selected? And, how much power will the newbie have to shape the world agenda? That’s the topic of today’s First Edition. Before that, this morning’s headlines.
UK news | The Metropolitan police remains institutionally racist, misogynistic and homophobic three years after a damning review into the force’s culture, a report has found.

Technology | Chuck Schumer, the current US Senate minority leader, accused Jensen Huang, the newly reinstated Nvidia CEO, of shipping “extremely advanced chips to China” and violating US export control laws.
Benefits | Hundreds of thousands of people face losing their disability benefits under plans being considered by ministers as part of a shake-up of the welfare system.

A crucial vote for the next UN chief was due to take place this Friday. Now, the vote has been delayed to allow for last-minute negotiations.

After a multiyear process of nominations, hustings and endless lobbying, on Monday members of the 15-strong security council will once again be polled on where their support lies. There are eight candidates still in the running – each hopeful will receive an “encourage”, “discourage” or “no opinion” label from each voting member in a non-binding sense check.

It’s a voting system that makes the Vatican’s smoke-based setup seem logical and easy to follow. Early straw polls treat all 15 members equally, without distinguishing between security council’s five permanent members (the P5: Britain, China, France, Russia and the US) and its 10 elected members (E10).While individual responses are not revealed, colour-coded ballot papers will show where a verdict has come from: P5 nations will have red paperwork; the 10 elected members (E10) will have white documents. This isn’t simply to add some pizazz: while a candidate only needs nine endorsements to succeed, a “discourage” from one of the P5 blocks their path with an effective veto. And this is the process post-democratisation.

Until now, the contest has been led by Rebeca Grynspan. Since 30 July, there have been eight of these secret straw polls – Grynspan came out on top in seven. With the security council’s blessing, a recommended candidate is presented to the general assembly in what is ostensibly a rubber-stamping exercise. Only, recent events have set Grynspan’s campaign off-course, as the process has become rather messy.

Grynspan – a 70-year-old economist and career diplomat – is secretary-general of the UN’s Trade and Development body (Unctad), and is a former vice-president of Costa Rica. If successful, she would be the first woman in the job, and the first Jewish person (her parents were refugees who fled Poland for Costa Rica in the 1930s).

“She has run an incremental, old-school campaign that convinced almost all security council members that she could do the job,” Richard Gowan, a UN-expert with the International Crisis Group tells me from New York. She has secured backing from the UK, France and China, but not (yet) the US or Russia. While in the last straw poll, Grynspan secured 10 votes – more than the requisite nine – two rejections likely came from these veto-wielding members.

“This opposition does not appear to stem from a fundamental dislike of her,” says Gowan. “US diplomats have kept open the possibility of working with her if she ends up as the last candidate standing, but rather because Washington and Moscow now favour an alternative.” Experts have suggested US reservations may stem from criticism emerging from Unctad towards Israel, and Russia’s from her comments on Moscow suspending grain shipments through the Black Sea.

For months, Grynspan’s main rival was Argentina’s Rafael Mariano Grossi, the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) director general. But in the last month, two new candidates entered the race. Turkey’s Feridun Hadi Sinirlioğlu (who flopped), and Lana Nusseibeh from the UAE, whose bid has proved more successful. Nusseibeh is now said to have the backing of the US and Russia. She had been waiting in the wings for months before launching her eleventh-hour candidacy.

“Initially, observers assumed she would wrap up the selection quickly with all veto powers on board,” says Gowan. Only, it hasn’t proved so simple. Beijing remains sceptical of her, in part because the US and Russia failed to consult China, and concern over the UAE’s recent proximity to the US administration. Nusseibeh has also faced significant criticism from civil society groups, citing her denials of accusations that the UAE is fuelling the war in Sudan by supporting paramilitaries. It is believed to have significantly influenced London and Paris in opposing her candidacy. Earlier this month, 68 British MPs wrote to Andy Burnham calling on him to veto Nusseibeh, describing her as “a tainted and compromised figure”.

There had been a prolonged pause in straw-polling activities before last week – the presumption being that, behind closed doors, the powers that be were convening to come up with a compromise. There was even speculation that Vladimir Putin, Xi Jinping and Donald Trump had discussed the matter at their uneventful Shenzhen trilateral, though no breakthrough materialised. The dynamics are unusually complicated because the coalitions vary by candidate.

Secret meetings are rumbling on. Nusseibeh is on a charm offensive in London. The next vote being pushed back beyond this weekend suggests a deal might be in the offing. Gowan still believes a consensus will be reached. “None of the P5 members desire the embarrassment of failing,” he says. Many of the UN’s 193 members argue the selection process allows five countries to wield outsized influence. “A failure to reach agreement would simply signal that the P5 is incapable of running the UN,” says Gowan.

That said, the clock is ticking. And it is a sign of how strained international relations are that we’ve reached this crisis point. While negotiations did go to the wire during the cold war, the two most recent sec-gens had been anointed by October. There are now high-level talks about what further deadlock might mean: An interim boss or committee of senior officials could manage affairs until the race’s conclusion, but it’s uncharted territory. (This report sets out the options.)
Despite Guterres’s 2023 assertion that the top job “has no power at all”, the fight to replace him is significant.

The UN has faced a bruising decade: it has looked impotent as wars and genocides have seen states show disregard for the international law it’s tasked with upholding; there’s been talk of bankruptcy. In diplomatic circles, Guterres is widely viewed as having been too risk-averse on peace and security. “Consequently, all leading contenders are pledging to step up mediation efforts and restore morale within a dispirited institution,” says Gowan.

There are also distinct differences to their platforms. Grynspan emphasises structural reform, but has championed similar causes to the departing boss: climate and sustainable development. Grossi has largely avoided climate change to align with current US administration priorities. Nusseibeh has questioned the future of the UN’s traditional approach to development amid shrinking international aid budgets.

Ian Martin worked for the UN for more than 20 years. He was the special representative of the secretary-general in Timor-Leste (formerly East Timor), Nepal and then Libya. Today, he chairs the board of the United Nations Association. I ask him what’s at stake in this selection. “The choice matters immensely,” he says. The secretary-general isn’t simply an administrator or manager subordinate to the security council and general assembly. “They are a principal organ of the UN entrusted with peace and security responsibilities,” says Martin.

They might not command a military, he concedes, “but the office carries substantial moral authority and provides direct conflict mediation. While deep geopolitical divides in the security council have hindered effective UN action on crises such as Ukraine and Gaza, this deadlock makes an independent, proactive secretary-general even more critical.”

Trump makes millions after pressuring Nvidia to reinstate Huang

Jensen Huang has been reinstated as CEO of AI chip powerhouse Nvidia, just 11 days after his resignation. As the chip firm’s share price soared, Guardian columnist and Politics Weekly America host Jonathan Freedland tells Lucy Hough how Trump made millions overnight.
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

The Pitt Rivers Museum in Oxford has one of the largest-known collections artefacts from Nagaland, a mountainous state in north-eastern India – and, until very recently, it also held human remains of the people who lived there, including those of two children, a woman and a village chief. Now, after 80 years of display on crowded glass shelves, those remains are being afforded their dignity and repatriated to India.

Our sibling newsletter This Is India (sign up here) explains that – unlike countries such as Australia, Canada and the US – India has no national laws for the repatriation of Indigenous ancestral remains. Thus a six-year process of negotiation led to the museum handing custodianship to a Naga delegation of leaders and scholars earlier this month. “The question,” writes Niha Masih, “is about the right to honour the ancestors and give them a dignified resting place.”
