articles.title: ‘The whole process just doesn’t work’: claimants relive the agonies of Pip assessments
articles.summary: Applicants recount a catalogue of problems including tedious award reviews for sufferers of severe lifelong conditions
body: Rob Denholm clearly remembers his first personal independence payment (Pip) assessment, when he was asked more than 90 questions in 55 minutes.

“You’re constantly asked the same question in a different way. I remember thinking, I must not have answered that properly, so you try and find a different way to answer. And by doing that, you’re working against yourself,” he said. “The assessor didn’t know about my cognitive impairment, and I couldn’t find the words to explain.”
The 46-year-old from Warrington, who has multiple sclerosis (MS), was denied the level of Pip he applied for, and was forced to spend six months going through a tribunal process which he won.
“They said I navigated the test centre well, despite falling into a chair,” he said. “The whole process just doesn’t work. You can’t assess fluctuating conditions in a 45-minute interview.”

In the first comprehensive review of Pip since it was launched in 2013, the disability minister Sir Stephen Timms has concluded it is “dehumanising” and “no longer fit for purpose”, and recommended a range of reforms.

These include a fast-track route to Pip for people with severe, lifelong conditions, and reducing unnecessary award reviews for people whose health conditions are lifelong, progressive or unlikely to improve.

He also suggested moving away from rigid, tick-box assessments that only capture a snapshot of a person’s condition on a particular day, but to consider the broader financial and practical barriers that caused a person’s disability.
The news was warmly welcomed by Denholm, who said he had struggled to get assessors to understand that the symptoms he experiences fluctuate daily.

“There needs to be more flexibility and understanding that conditions don’t present themselves in the same way all of the time,” said Denholm, who contributed his views to the review through the Multiple Sclerosis Society. “They asked me, ‘Can you walk 50 metres?’ I said, well there are days I can walk that, but there are also days I can’t guarantee I’ll make it back again.
“It’s like looking out the window to see what the weather’s doing, and then using that as a mark of what it’s going to be doing in March.”

The Timms review comes just over a week after Alan Milburn published his recommendations on how to get the country’s 1 million young people who are not in education, employment or training (Neet) back into work.

He suggested a complete overhaul of the system for under-25s, in which they would no longer qualify for Pip or the health element of universal credit, and would instead get a new youth allowance paid at the standard rate of universal credit.

“Pip assessments are broken at the moment,” said 22-year-old Caroline*, who has osteogenesis imperfecta (OI), also known as brittle bone disease. “You have to go through all this rigmarole with someone who seems like they’re trying to catch you out.”
Caroline’s disability is lifelong, and she said she breaks on average a bone once a year. Despite knowing her condition is incurable, she goes through Pip reassessment every few years.
Timms’s recommendation to end repeat assessments for people with lifelong or degenerative conditions would repair a process Caroline calls “ludicrous”.

“I’ve had brittle bone disease since I was born. It’s not a condition there is a cure for, it’s never going away. I will always be disabled,” she said. “Something I dread every few years is reapplying for Pip. It’s humiliating to try and convince someone over the phone that I am still disabled.”
The extra costs of her disability, which Pip helps her cover, include using public transport and taxis because of her physical fragility and chronic fatigue, as well as having to pay for medication.

But she felt Milburn’s idea of removing Pip from under-25s would be unhelpful. “It’s the worst time to take support away, because at least when I was under 16, I lived with my parents,” she said. “Now I live alone. I need the money even more. So I don’t know why cutting support for 16 to 25-year-olds is meant to help anyone.”
Related: What are the proposals for changing personal independence payment?
Caroline’s symptoms fluctuate – sometimes her day is “very similar to a non-disabled person’s average day” but other days she experiences heightened symptoms.

Beth Harris, 26, who was diagnosed with stage 2 non-Hodgkin lymphoma in March last year, applied for Pip as soon as she was able to. She had just started chemotherapy and was having to cover the additional costs of taxis to and from hospital, as well as adaptations at home.

Her initial application was rejected because she had been told her illness was not expected to last more than six months. But it did last longer and she was granted Pip, although she wasn’t given backdated payments for the previous months.
In the interim, her grandmother helped her cover the extra cost of taxis.

“She’s 89, she’s on a pension, so we found it really difficult,” she said. “If they just remove that barrier and say, ‘OK, you’ve got cancer, we’ll start the claim, and we can review this once you finish your first lot of treatment’, that would make a massive difference.”
She says assessors should have “more training on cancer patients”.

“I think the biggest change there would need to be is to get rid of the requirement, especially for a cancer diagnosis, that you have to be ill for at least six months, because no one knows how an individual’s going to respond to cancer treatment until they’ve had it done,” she said.
Lauren Marks, head of policy at Young Lives vs Cancer, said young people with cancer were not a long-term benefit claimant population and could be adversely affected by Milburn’s proposed changes.

“That severe conditions criteria predicates that the condition has to be lifelong and deteriorating, and that’s just not cancer,” she said. “But I think you’d be hard pressed to find somebody who doesn’t think that cancer in a young person is a severe condition when it’s happening to them.”
Names have been changed for anonymity

articles.title: ‘They don’t believe in freedom’: Yemenis plan their escape as Houthis advance on Aden
articles.summary: With Iran’s proxy fighters encircling the temporary capital, residents and NGOs prepare to evacuate
body: Hussein fled his home six years ago after it fell under Houthi control, moving as far south as he could to the port city of Aden, where there was a measure of safety.
The Saudi-backed Yemeni government had made the city its temporary capital; the hundreds of kilometres between it and the Houthis were well fortified.

Today, Hussein is once again considering the painful decision of leaving home. In September, the Iran-aligned Houthis swept aside Yemeni government forces, and now have set their sights on Aden. Houthi fighters are amassing to the north and east of the city, and have begun encircling the government-controlled territory.

“I fled my home in Sana’a and came here. I don’t think the Houthis plan to take over Aden right now, but if they get closer, I will have no choice but to flee again to Marib or Hadhramaut,” said Hussein, who was speaking under a pseudonym.

Hussein works as a schoolteacher and was formerly a member of the Islah party, an Islamist political party aligned with Saudi Arabia that is in opposition to the Houthi movement. He fears that if the Houthis take control of Aden he could face persecution for his former affiliation.
“The Houthis don’t believe in freedom, they just want to hear one voice, the one they like,” he said.

Hussein is one of many residents and organisations nervously watching the Houthi advance. The militia is still about 50 miles (80km) north of Aden, but local people fear government forces may not be able to resist another Houthi assault, having seen the dramatic collapse of government forces and allied militias in September.

Aden has been the seat of the Saudi-backed government of Yemen since 2015. If the Houthis took the city, it would be a huge blow for the government, and a massive failure for the Saudi-led coalition which has for years fought against the Houthis.
The 12-year-long civil war would tilt dramatically in the Houthis’ favour and be a boon for Iran, which has long invested military and political support in the insurgent movement.

The Yemeni government has pulled back many of its fighters to help defend Aden and the surrounding areas, announcing last week that fighters were redeployed from areas along the south-western coast towards the port city.

Saudi Arabia has tried to halt the Houthi advance with a renewed bombing campaign, carrying out hundreds of airstrikes in Yemen since September, killing and wounding 822 civilians, including 181 children, according to statistics from the independent Yemen Data Project.
Houthi authorities have alleged that Saudi Arabia has carried out 5,500 air and missile attacks since July.

The Houthis have not announced any intention to take Aden, but have instead been amassing troops north of Kirish, and in al-Bayda, areas which, if taken, would cut off the northern and eastern roads to Aden.
“The buildups in al-Bayda could threaten Aden’s eastern road links through Abyan and Saudi supply lines into the city,” said Mohammed al-Basha, the founder of the US-based risk advisory Basha Report.

“The Houthis appear to be testing how well Aden’s defences will hold. If they collapse, the Houthis could try to seize the city. If government forces hold, the Houthis could try to lay siege to it,” al-Basha added.

Houthi forces have begun striking Aden and its surrounding areas, rupturing the relative safety the city has offered for years. Residents have watched anxiously as explosions grow nearer, and displaced people from surrounding areas have started to arrive in greater numbers.
“Since last week, we’ve started following the news every hour. When I get busy, I tell my daughter to follow it and update me,” said Rami, a resident of Aden who spoke under a pseudonym.

The 53-year-old bitterly recalled his experience during the four-month battle for Aden in 2015, when he was stuck in the crossfire between the Houthis and Yemeni government forces. He, like other people in Aden, is trying to make his own calculation of when, or if, the Houthis will arrive.
International organisations are also making contingency plans in case of a Houthi takeover of the city.

“We were informed by management that they are issuing termination notices to all staff this week. If the Houthis don’t reach Aden, they will continue operations and renew our contracts; otherwise this is the end of the road,” an aid worker with an international NGO said.
Already, several NGOs were forced to shut down in the city of Taiz after sweeping Houthi gains.

Not all NGOs would leave in the case of a Houthi takeover, but some are unable to work in Houthi-controlled areas either due to fears for the safety of aid workers, or because the US Treasury designated the Houthis a foreign terrorist organisation in 2025.
Yemen has for years faced a severe humanitarian crisis, with about 18.7 million people facing acute food insecurity.

Fighting has only exacerbated conditions, severing transport routes, pushing up the prices of goods and worsening the country’s displacement crisis – including more than 350,000 people displaced since August.

“I earn daily wages, and when there is no work, my six family members don’t get enough food,” said Ahmed, a restaurant worker in his 50s. “I don’t care about politics or wars, and I’m not involved in any of it. I’m just like millions of Yemenis struggling to provide basic necessities for their families.”
For many of Aden’s residents, the prospect of a Houthi takeover has shattered the sense of safety that they sought by coming to the government stronghold in the first place.

“I’m not stocking up on food because I won’t stay in Aden and wait for the battles to reach the city. It isn’t only me; my family is also ready to flee at any time … staying at home won’t be safe and we might get trapped,” Rami said.

articles.title: In charts: how power could shift in Europe’s big year of elections
articles.summary: More than half of EU voters will go to the polls in the next 12 months, with the far right targeting significant gains. We set out the political landscape and trends
body: Over the coming 12 months, more than half of the EU’s electorate will go to the polls in elections that could change the direction of the continent, with attention focused on voters in four of the bloc’s five biggest states.

In Spain, France and Poland, elections could bring the far right into government. Italy’s far-right prime minister looks likely to remain in power, but is under pressure from a challenger even further to the right.

While few of Europe’s far-right parties want to leave the EU, they still see the bloc as a top-down project that undermines national sovereignty and are bent on transforming it into something far looser. The graphics below map the main political parties in each country along two ideological axes – economic left-right and libertarian-authoritarian – using data from researchers at the Chapel Hill Expert Survey. Polling averages then show how the race is developing.
Parliamentary election on 29 November
Spain will head to the polls on Sunday to vote in a sixth general election in 11 years. The snap election could end eight years of socialist-led rule and bring a far-right party into government.

Since the restoration of democracy in Spain in 1977, every prime minister has come from one of three parties: the now-disbanded Union of the Democratic Centre, a very broad centrist alliance from the time of the transition; the centre-right People’s party (PP); and the centre-left Socialist Workers’ party (PSOE).

Often the ruling party has needed the support of smaller parties, sometimes regional groups. But, as elsewhere in Europe, the traditional centre-right and centre-left parties are being challenged by populists further to the left and right.

Since 2023, Pedro Sánchez has been in government with the support of Sumar, which sits ideologically to the left of his PSOE party. But polling suggests that PSOE and Sumar’s latest incarnation, Broad Front, will together fail to muster a majority in parliament.

That leaves the door partly open to the PP, led by Alberto Núñez Feijóo, but he too will need support, and just as Sánchez looked to his left, it is thought Feijóo will look to his right, bringing the far-right Vox of Santiago Abascal into government. Abascal this week told a rally that “remigration sounds to me like heavenly music”.

Presidential election on 18 April and 2 May 2027The sitting president, Emmanuel Macron, has served the maximum two terms and will be an onlooker in next spring’s election. If, as usual, no candidate wins 50% in the first round of voting, the two leading candidates go into a runoff two weeks later. Polling suggests that Marine Le Pen, the leader of the far-right Rassemblement National (the National Rally) will be one of those two, for the third time.

But unlike on previous occasions, there is no obvious centrist candidate to challenge her in the second round. The president’s heirs apparent – Gabriel Attal of Macron’s Renaissance party and Édouard Philippe of coalition partners Horizons – are splitting the centrist vote. Both were prime ministers under Macron – but then so were five other politicians.

Raphaël Glucksmann, a former Socialist who left to found his own party, is nonetheless the Socialist and centre-left candidate. He is outflanked on the left by Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who seems most likely to face Le Pen in the second round. In the contest between the far left and far right, the polls suggest Le Pen will be the victor.
Parliamentary election expected by November 2027

For 20 years, the prime ministers of Poland have come from one of two parties, the hard-right Law and Justice (PiS) party, or the Civic Platform – now Civic Coalition (KO) – of Donald Tusk, a centrist and relatively libertarian party which is in government. The two parties’ starkly opposing ideas and practices have led to constitutional crisis, not least because PiS holds the presidency.

Although polling shows support for PiS faltering, Tusk can take little comfort – much of that support seems to be flowing toward parties even farther to the right; Konfederacja (Confederation), a libertarian nationalist far-right coalition, and their former allies, the Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP). KKP was last assessed by Chapel Hill researchers in 2024 as part of Konfederacja, but the party is significantly further to the authoritarian right. It is also the only party that advocates Poland’s withdrawal from the EU and faces regular criticism for pro-Russian positions on foreign policy.

Even worse for Tusk, two of his three coalition partners – the centre-right Polska 2050 and the conservative agrarian PSL – are at risk of polling below the 5% threshold needed to enter parliament. Their success or failure in clearing that threshold could play a major role in deciding the election.

Parliamentary election due by 22 December 2027The last of the big four is Italy, where the far right has been in power since 2022. Giorgia Meloni’s Fratelli d’Italia (Brothers of Italy) party has been in a rightwing coalition with Lega (League) and the relatively centrist Forza Italia.
Meloni is odds on to remain prime minister after the election, according to the Polymarket betting site. But she is under pressure, perhaps surprisingly, from the right.

Roberto Vannacci, a retired general, has started a far-right party, Futuro Nazionale (National Future), and is polling at least as well as Meloni’s coalition partners. Vannacci’s party is too new to have been assessed by Chapel Hill researchers, but given that his stated reason for leaving Lega was that it was insufficiently rightwing, it is very probably in the upper right quadrant of the chart.

articles.title: Colombia’s president arrives at scene of supermarket hostage siege in tourist city
articles.summary: Abelardo de la Espriella to take control of operation trying to free at least 20 hostages
body: Colombia’s president has arrived at the scene of an hours-long standoff between security services and gunmen holding at least 20 people hostage inside a supermarket in Cartagena, a popular tourist city.

Abelardo de la Espriella’s motorcade arrived in Cartagena on Tuesday night, Agence France-Presse reported, where he will ostensibly take control of an operation involving scores of officers, the navy and special forces.
About 30 people were initially seized by the armed men early on Tuesday morning, but by nightfall, 10 hostages – five of them elderly women – had been released, police said.
There have been no reports of injuries so far.

Before arriving in Cartagena, the rightwing president said that, despite the context of growing violence perpetrated by criminal groups involved in the country’s decades-long armed conflict, the hostage-taking appeared to have stemmed from a botched robbery carried out by “common criminals”.
The past few days have been particularly challenging in the South American country, with a car bomb and a drone attack killing one person and leaving nearly 30 injured.

The supermarket where the hostages are being held is just six miles from the old city and its 500-year-old fortress walls overlooking the Caribbean. Hundreds of thousands of visitors are drawn to Cartagena every year.

The gunmen reportedly arrived at about 8.30am local time at an Éxito supermarket in La Castellana neighbourhood and, according to Colombia’s president, the group planned to rob an armoured cash-in-transit vehicle that was due to collect the previous day’s takings from the store.
After spotting the movement on security cameras, employees reportedly alerted the national police, who surrounded the supermarket.

“My son is there,” Jacob Pérez, the father of one of the workers reportedly held hostage, told Agence France-Presse. “He didn’t leave work and he’s not answering his phone. I think they took it from him,” he said.
Customers were also believed to be among the hostages. The five people initially released were “older women”, according to De la Espriella.

Footage shared on social media showed dozens of people rushing out of the supermarket, while local media outlets showed snipers positioned on nearby buildings in what appeared to be a standoff between the armed men and police.

De la Espriella, known for his populist rhetoric and an “iron fist” approach to crime – he sometimes wears a gun on his waist and has posed beside the bodies of people killed by police – has been in office for just over three months, and said the hours-long standoff at the supermarket “will turn out well for the hostages, but I’m not so sure it will turn out quite so well for the hostage-takers”.

He addressed the case at a press conference in Villavicencio, about 684 miles inland, where he was dealing with the aftermath of an attack on Monday night in which a car bomb was detonated outside the headquarters of the Meta departmental government.
More than 20 people were injured and a security guard was killed, and the president attributed the attack to a dissident faction of the Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (Farc).

“Narco-terrorism is desperate because we are confronting it decisively. It intends to intimidate us and force us to retreat in search of another false peace process,” the president said, referring to the landmark 2016 peace deal between the government and the Farc – the 10th anniversary of whose signing was on Tuesday.

Internationally recognised for substantially reducing violence, the deal alone could not bring the decades-long armed conflict to a definitive end. Subsequent administrations were slow to implement the agreement, which was rejected by Farc dissidents and other rebel factions.

In the early hours of Monday, in another part of the country, gunmen believed to belong to the ELN, an armed group that never signed a peace deal, used drones to drop bombs on the local police command in the city of Cúcuta. Instead they hit homes and injured three civilians, including an 18-month-old baby.
Although drone attacks by criminal groups have become increasingly common, it was the first time they had targeted a departmental capital.

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy and Hungary PM hail new era of cooperation after Orbán
articles.summary: Hungary’s new PM, Péter Magyar, calls for efforts ‘to build trust’ with Kyiv after ousting of pro-Kremlin predecessor Viktor Orbán. What we know on day 1,736
body: Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Hungary’s Péter Magyar held talks in west Ukraine on Tuesday, with both hailing a new era in ties after years of tension under Budapest’s previous pro-Kremlin ruler Viktor Orbán. Tuesday’s meeting was billed as central to Kyiv’s hopes of accelerating its EU membership bid and strengthening economic ties with central Europe. Magyar, a pro-EU conservative who took office in May, met Zelenskyy in the war-torn country’s westernmost region of Transcarpathia – also home to a Hungarian ethnic minority. “This is an important moment and it is … very sensitive,” Zelenskyy said in a press conference, alongside Magyar, in the border town of Berehove, describing their talks as “positive”. The Hungarian prime minister said it was “in the interests of all neighbours to maintain good relations with one another”. He added: “I am very grateful that you have been able to achieve this; let us begin to build trust – better late than never.”

Zelenskyy said the two leaders discussed an ‌increase in Hungary’s diesel exports to Ukraine as well as use of Ukrainian gas storage facilities by Hungarian companies. Energy and agriculture ministers from the two countries will meet to discuss projects, Magyar said, while Budapest was also open to joining the Carpathian Eight grouping of regional countries launched by Zelenskyy, the Hungarian premier added. The two leaders also agreed to an expansion of rail transport between their countries, Zelenskyy said, without providing further details.

Ukraine’s foreign minister said a drone attack against a Russian military vessel and cargo ship in Libyan waters at the ⁠weekend, which killed two ⁠Libyan army personnel, was a legitimate act of ⁠self-defence. Reacting to criticism from Libya’s ​western-backed government of national unity about being dragged into the war, Andrii Sybiha said Russian naval vessels and cargo ships transporting military equipment were valid targets and Ukraine’s right to self-defence was enshrined in Article 51 of the United Nations charter. “Ukraine respects the sovereignty and ‌territorial integrity of Libya,” Khmara said on Telegram. “We emphasise that Ukraine’s actions are aimed at countering Russian armed aggression and are not intended to harm Libya or its people.”

The eastern-based ‌Libyan National ‌Army (LNA) General Command, which control’s the east of the country and has ties with Russia, on Tuesday said a ‌response to the Ukrainian attack would come “at ​the appropriate time and place”.

Norway and Ukraine ⁠will expand their cooperation on a newly developed anti-drone air defence system, the Norwegian Defence Ministry ⁠said on Tuesday. Known as DESNA, it was developed by Norwegian defence technology company ⁠Kongsberg and a Ukrainian partner, the ministry said. The two countries want to expand the system – which consists of Ukrainian-made air defence ⁠missiles and launch units linked to Kongsberg control systems donated ​by Norway to more parts ‌of Ukraine. Ukrainian Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said the system had demonstrated its ability to destroy drones, including jet-powered drones that ‌Russian forces are deploying in increasing numbers.

Belarusian president Alexander Lukashenko, a close ally of Russian leader Vladimir Putin, has proposed he and Zelenskyy fly together to Moscow for talks to end the war. Lukashenko, who allowed Russia to ⁠use his country’s territory for ⁠the February ​2022 invasion of Ukraine, told the French media outlet Le Point on Tuesday that he believed Russian forces were winning on the battlefield. “Zelenskyy and I could simply go and fly to Moscow. ​The two of us. As a guarantor ‌of his safety, I ‌could sit with him and fly to Moscow,” Lukashenko said in comments reported by Belarus’ state Belta ‌news agency. Zelenskyy has said he is prepared to meet ⁠Putin in a neutral location.

Ukraine has continued attacks ⁠on Russian oil refineries despite ⁠requests from Donald Trump to refrain, Putin said on Tuesday, pledging to retaliate. Kyiv has said it would stop striking Russian energy targets only when Moscow ⁠did the same. “We see that the Kyiv ⁠regime continues to attack our refining facilities, despite the US president’s appeal and direct request to refrain from such ​attacks. But the Kyiv authorities are ignoring this advice,” ‌Putin told a meeting of government ‌officials and senior oil executives in the Kremlin. “In this regard, I would like to stress that retaliatory measures ‌on our part are inevitable,” he said.

articles.title: Australia’s security pact with Solomon Islands a blow to China’s influence in the Pacific
articles.summary: Anthony Albanese and Matthew Wale sign new treaty as Solomon Islands PM states his country no longer ‘a source of uncertainty and doubt in the region’
body: The Solomon Islands prime minister says the days of his country being an uncertain partner in the Pacific are over as he signed a sweeping agreement to make Australia his country’s primary security partner and limit ties with China.

Matthew Wale signed the new treaty with Australia’s prime minister, Anthony Albanese, in Canberra on Wednesday after Solomon Islands earlier this week announced it was terminating a landmark security pact with Beijing.
The deal includes $740m in new funding from Australia over 10 years, comprising $670m in grants and $70m in loans. Money is expected to flow from January.

The treaty is a blow to China’s efforts to build influence with Pacific Island nations and a major win for the Albanese government’s campaign to rebuild ties across the region. A backlash is expected from Beijing, which has used missile tests and military exercises to express its displeasure in the past.
Related: Inflation rate jumps to 4.9% as Australia’s cost-of-living crisis intensifies
“Solomon Islands has been, for a number of years, a source of uncertainty and doubt in the region,” Wale said. “Those days are done. Gone. We don’t want to be there again.”

The deal means Solomon Islands will not allow foreign military bases or major security infrastructure to be developed on its territory. Sensitive systems will remain “free from militarisation, any form of foreign interference or unauthorised access”.
Chinese police officers are expected to leave Solomon Islands by the middle of 2027. About 14 officers have been posted to the country under the expiring deal with Beijing.

Honiara has secured new funding from Australia for policing services and improved visa arrangements, allowing Solomon Islands citizens to stay in Australia for longer periods. An expansion of the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) scheme is planned to allow Solomons citizens to work in early childhood education and aged care.
Australia’s funding will help provide universal access to education, from kindergarten to year 12. A third of Solomon Islands children do not attend school and less than 20% complete year 12.

Australia and Solomon Islands have agreed to advance joint economic, development and security priorities through the deal, with Australia pledging to invest in community development, education and infrastructure.
Australia will also increase funding for the Solomon Kings football club, including player development.
“This treaty will strengthen our security partnership,” Albanese said.

“Australia is proud to be Solomon Islands’ main security partner, and that’s a responsibility that we take seriously. We’ll continue working with Solomon Islands to keep its community safe, to strengthen its police force and improve border security.
“We’ll do that in a way that completely respects Solomon Islands sovereignty and its right to make its own decisions.”
Wale said secrecy provisions prevented him from speaking publicly when asked about ending the pact with Beijing. The five-year deal was due to expire in April and will not be renewed.
“We have ongoing discussions with China, but of course today is about our relationship with Australia and the treaty that we’ve signed,” he said.

Albanese welcomed more than 15 Solomon Island cabinet ministers as part of the official delegation visiting Canberra. Their presence and Wale’s confidence at surviving any fresh no confidence motions in parliament signalled the stronger relationship could last.

Albanese and senior Australian ministers including Penny Wong, Pat Conroy and Richard Marles stepped up engagement in the Pacific after Labor’s election win in 2022. Labor has signed new alliances and agreements with countries including Papua New Guinea, Tuvalu, Vanuatu and Fiji.

The Coalition could oppose the new treaty because of language about a transition to net zero carbon emissions by 2050. Earlier this week, the opposition said it would not support Australia’s Nakamal agreement with Vanuatu on similar grounds. It said future governments should not be bound to energy policy settings because of foreign treaties.

Asked about the termination of the Solomon Islands deal, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson, Guo Jiakun, said on Tuesday that no element of geopolitical rivalry or bloc confrontation existed in Beijing’s cooperation with the Pacific.
“China always follows the principle of mutual respect and equality in developing relations with the Solomon Islands.
“Our cooperation does not target any third party and is not subject to third-party influence.”
China’s embassy in Canberra was contacted for comment.

articles.title: China investigates politburo star in Xi Jinping’s latest purge
articles.summary: Chen Jining, regarded as a contender for higher office, becomes the fourth member of China’s elite politburo to be investigated since 2025
body: China has launched an investigation into Shanghai’s Communist party chief Chen Jining, a member of the country’s elite politburo, the state-run Xinhua news agency unexpectedly announced on Tuesday, marking the fourth member of the top leadership ⁠body to be probed since ⁠2025.
China’s anti-graft watchdog is investigating ​Chen for “suspected severe violations of discipline and laws”, Xinhua said, using a common euphemism for corruption.

For Chinese officials, especially those of Chen’s ⁠rank, the public announcement of an investigation by the central commission for discipline inspection generally signals their eventual political downfall.
The investigation marks a further escalation in President Xi Jinping’s widening anti-graft campaign, which has thinned the party’s senior leadership ranks and depleted the military’s top command.
Related: Fate of China’s top general more likely to do with power struggle than corruption
Before the announcement of the Chen probe, three politburo members from the once 24-member body formed in 2022 – He Weidong, Zhang ⁠Youxia and Ma Xingrui – had already been purged.

Chen, 62, had an unusual rise through China’s official ranks. ​An environmental scientist by training, he earned a doctorate from Imperial ‌College London and rose through China’s elite Tsinghua ‌University to become its president.

He entered government as China’s environmental protection minister in 2015 – just as Xi was elevating pollution control and ecological protection as ‌policy priorities – before becoming mayor of Beijing. He joined the politburo in 2022 and was named party boss of Shanghai, China’s financial hub.
He has long been viewed as a political star and a plausible contender for higher national office. The investigation into him took analysts by surprise.

The hashtag “Chen Jining under investigation” had amassed about 240m views on the Chinese microblogging platform Weibo by Wednesday morning, with many users saying they were “shocked” and “stunned” in comments under state media posts.
“This is arguably the biggest political news to come out of China in a few years,” Taisu Zhang, a professor at Yale Law School specialising in contemporary Chinese law and politics, wrote on X.
Zhang pointed to Chen’s status as a rising political star who had been seen as “a near-lock for the politburo Standing Committee”, China’s highest political decision-making body.

At a gathering of leaders last month, the ruling Communist party pledged to keep waging indefinitely its high-pressure anti-corruption campaign, which has ensnared millions within ‌China’s vast bureaucracy and has seen hundreds of top officials purged, including those once thought untouchable.

Xi had called on the party to “turn the blade inward” and unleash a revolution on itself and eradicate “viruses and impurities” that corrode its health. The party views ​the drive as essential to ensuring its long-term survival.
“No matter who they are, how high their position, or how great their contributions, anyone who engages in corruption will surely receive no leniency,” Xi said in January.

Chen’s unexpected probe “sends a signal that there’s no letting up in the anti-corruption drive and the party’s ‘self-revolution,’” said China expert Jean Christopher Mittelstaedt of the University of Zurich.
“If anything, it continues to intensify.”
The Shanghai party secretary post is one of China’s most prestigious provincial-level positions and has often served as a springboard to top leadership roles.
Xi himself briefly served as Shanghai’s party boss in 2007 before joining the politburo’s standing committee, the country’s highest decision-making body.

“Chen Jining is no ordinary fallen official … [He is] an exemplar of someone who rose from the specialised field of environmental protection to the pinnacle of political power,” Mao Shoulong, a professor of public administration and policy at Renmin University of China, wrote in a commentary on WeChat.

“His downfall, therefore, is not merely that of an individual, but of an entire type of official, a model of political advancement, and a set of assumptions about the relationship between technology and politics, expertise and power, and competence and loyalty,” Mao wrote.

Shanghai’s senior party leadership pledged loyalty to Beijing and understanding of the need to “see things through ⁠to the end” ⁠after Chen ​was put under investigation, the financial hub’s official paper said on Wednesday.

articles.title: Why is France fighting Vanuatu over two uninhabited islands in the Pacific?
articles.summary: The battle over the Matthew and Hunter islands – and their 350,000 sq km economic zone – has made its way to the UN’s highest court
body: Two tiny specks of volcanic land in the vast Pacific Ocean – home to seabirds and not much else – are at the centre of an escalating territorial battle between France and Vanuatu.

The decades-long dispute over the Matthew and Hunter islands has entered a new phase, with Vanuatu launching two separate international legal proceedings against France as part of its attempt to claim these Pacific territories. Arbitration proceedings began last month, which could threaten France’s claim to a vast expanse of the ocean surrounding the islands.
At stake is an exclusive economic zone of roughly 350,000 sq km – almost the size of Germany – and the valuable fisheries and underwater resources stored within it.

The Matthew and Hunter islands – which Vanuatu calls Umaenupne and Umaeneg or Leka – are located east of Australia in the Pacific Ocean, just south of Vanuatu. Together, the two islands cover just 1.3 sq km and are uninhabited.

France claims the islands and the waters surrounding them as part of New Caledonia, a French Pacific territory, while Vanuatu argues they belong to its southernmost island communities, whose Indigenous people have maintained cultural and customary connections to the islands for centuries.
The waters surrounding the islands could also hold enormous economic value, according to Donald Rothwell, distinguished professor of international law at the Australian National University.
“The maritime entitlements and the resource sovereignty that goes with those islands would far outstrip the land value,” Rothwell said.
These “maritime entitlements” – currently claimed by France – include the exclusive economic zone of around the islands which gives potential access to valuable fisheries and seabed resources.
In the Pacific, France administers three territories – New Caledonia, French Polynesia, and Wallis and Futuna.
Vanuatu was jointly administered by France and Britain until gaining independence in 1980. Even then, Paris and London argued over who owned Matthew and Hunter Islands.

Since independence, Vanuatu has asserted its own claim, citing centuries of Indigenous cultural and economic ties to the islands. France meanwhile regularly conducts military expeditions there, and even established a meteorological facility on the islands.
Diplomatic efforts to resolve the disagreement intensified in recent years, including discussions between French president Emmanuel Macron and Vanuatu’s prime minister Jotham Napat in Paris in 2025.

Vanuatu has launched two separate legal proceedings against France: in August, the country filed an application with the international court of justice (ICJ), asking it to recognise its sovereignty over the islands. But the case cannot proceed unless France agrees to participate.
Last month Vanuatu also launched separate arbitration proceedings against Paris under the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (Unclos).

The legal action under Unclos could dramatically diminish the value of the islands, as Vanuatu is arguing they are not technically islands but merely rocks incapable of sustaining human life. Under international law, such rocks are entitled to just 12 nautical miles of territorial sea, a fraction of the territory France currently claims for fishing and resources around the islands.

Vanutau’s deputy prime minister Johnny Koanapo said the ICJ application filed in August is Paris’s “opportunity to demonstrate that France’s commitment to rules-based order is more than just rhetoric.”
“The islands have always been part of our history from time immemorial, before even the arrival of the colonial powers in Vanuatu,” Koanapo said.
He said securing sovereignty over the islands would mark “the completion of Vanuatu decolonisation”.
“We got our independence, but we have not gotten our entire territorial integrity back.”
France has consistently maintained that Matthew and Hunter are part of its territory, rejecting suggestions it should relinquish sovereignty over the islands.

In February the French foreign ministry said the long-running dispute had prevented the two countries from establishing a maritime boundary and created legal uncertainties affecting fishing and scientific research.
The Guardian sought comment from the governments of France and New Caledonia for this article, but neither responded before publication.
Rothwell sees the dispute between Vanuatu and France as part of a growing trend among Pacific island nations to challenge powerful countries in the courts.

“We’re seeing a much more assertive position being taken by small island states, in the Pacific in particular,” he said, pointing to Vanuatu’s successful campaign for a landmark ICJ advisory opinion on climate change.

But the claim has drawn criticism from pro-Paris politicians in New Caledonia. Nicolas Metzdorf, one of New Caledonia’s two representatives in France’s national assembly, dismissed the prospect of an international legal ruling on the islands’ sovereignty.
“I don’t really care about what the international organisation would say,” he said. “I defend my country’s interests.”
Vanuatu’s claim over the islands has also long been supported by New Caledonia’s indigenous Kanak independence movement, which has sought independence from France for decades.

articles.title: Canada says it ‘does not report to the US’ after Pentagon memo criticizing military spending
articles.summary: US document criticizes the supposedly ‘atrophied’ defence capabilities of its northern neighbour
body: Canada is a “sovereign nation” that does not “report” to the United States, the country’s defense minister said after the Pentagon released a scathing memo that criticized the supposedly “atrophied” defence capabilities of its northern neighbour.

The document, released Tuesday, said Canada had “yet to make the hard decisions and tradeoffs” necessary to meet previous defence spending pledges and become a “credible partner in the defense of our shared continent”.

The Pentagon memo said it took Canada nearly two decades to finally reach spending promises made in 2006 “despite Canada’s role as a major G7 economy as well as one of the largest and wealthiest members of the NATO alliance”.

Historically, Nato members have fallen short of meeting the security organization’s funding goals. When Russia annexed Crimea in 2014, only three Nato members – the US, the UK and Greece – were meeting the alliance’s guideline of spending 2% of GDP on defence. By 2025, all 31 members with armed forces, including Canada, had reached the goal.

The document also suggested Canada faces significant operational hurdles in its air, land and sea operations, blaming political leaders for pursuing “parochial economic and commercial interests over military optimization”.

The Pentagon document said the US defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, was “laser focused” on modernizing Canada’s military, suggesting American taxpayers had been “footing the bill for its defense” for decades.
The defense minister, David McGuinty, told reporters he could not “divine” the thinking behind the Pentagon’s decision to criticise Canada’s defence spending now.

“The amount of co-operation we are pushing under NORAD [North American Aerospace Defense Command] has not changed. What we’re doing together at Nato has not changed. Our military-to-military co-operation has not changed. Our work on integrated air missile defence has not changed,” he said.
McGuinty also bristled at the suggestion from a reporter that the memo implied Canada required approval from the US when it came to its spending plans.
“Canada is a sovereign nation. I’ll be very direct. We don’t report to the United States,” he said.
The memo came as a Canadian official travelled to Europe to pitch a new defence bank championed by the prime minister, Mark Carney.

Isabelle Hudon, Canada’s lead negotiator for establishing the Defence, Security and Resilience Bank, is looking to cajole more countries into joining a global initiative that would lend to governments and contractors at low cost to support defense projects.

Ten countries have pledged their support but no others from the G7 have done so yet, with both the UK and Germany so far declining to join. Hudon says the €4bn in commitments secured so far is enough to start the bank up but she is aiming for up to €100bn.

Carney has made significantly increased spending commitments in defence. The country spent $63.4bn on national defence in 2025, meeting its Nato pledge to spend 2% of gross domestic product for the first time.
Last year, Nato members agreed to raise the goal to the equivalent of 5% of GDP by 2035.

Canada’s federal budget this month laid out a plan to spend about 4% of Canada’s GDP on defence and security annually by the end of the decade, and 5% by 2035, including the purchase of submarines and early warning aircraft.

Canada’s air power is a key point of friction with Washington. Carney’s government has yet to make a final decision on its order of F-35 fighter jets from the US firm Lockheed Martin and is weighing the possibility of purchasing Swedish-made Gripen aircraft instead. The multibillion-dollar purchase has been the subject of a political review for more than a year. The Pentagon memo warned that operating a “mixed fleet” of aircraft would “compound existing personnel shortfalls”.

articles.title: Hundreds of thousands could lose disability benefits under Timms plans for Pip shake-up
articles.summary: Minister’s review says Pip system no longer fit for purpose and recommends new test for who is allowed to claim
body: Hundreds of thousands of people face losing their disability benefits under plans being considered by ministers as part of a shake-up of the welfare system.

Officials are drawing up plans to redesign the personal independence payment (Pip) system for adults in England and Wales after the work and pensions minister, Stephen Timms, deemed it “no longer fit for purpose”.
Timms recommended a new test for who should be allowed to claim Pip, which would exclude those who do not incur additional costs as a result of their disability.
Related: What are the proposals for changing personal independence payment?

According to a study by the Resolution Foundation, this would apply to as many as one in six of the 4 million people who claim the benefit – though officials stress they have not yet decided whether any cuts would apply to existing claimants or just new ones.
Timms told MPs on Tuesday: “The system is no longer fit for purpose and requires a fundamental reset.”

He added: “Support should correspond more closely to genuine additional costs and needs. Cumulative and fluctuating impacts should be recognised properly, and the highest support should reflect the most severe needs.”
Speaking on Tuesday morning, Timms’ co-author Sharon Brennan made clear some people were likely to see their payments cut.

“It’s likely there will be a rebalancing process in which some people will get more related to their needs, and some people therefore might get less,” she said. “But it’s for the government to make decisions based on our report about eligibility and what that cost should look like.”

Timms’ report is the second half of the government’s attempt to slow the speed at which the bill for disability benefits is climbing, with Pip forecast to rise from about £16bn in 2019-20 to just over £41bn by the end of the decade.

Last week a report by the former minister Alan Milburn recommended scrapping Pip entirely for under-25s and replacing it – as well as part of universal credit – with more concerted help to get back into work.

Timms rejected Milburn’s approach, saying Pip was still an important system for over-25s who claimed it, but he opened the door for the government to make cuts through a new assessment to see who should be allowed to claim and how much they should get.

He made two recommendations that have been immediately accepted by the government: to make it quicker for people with severe conditions to be able to claim Pip, and to reduce reviews for those whose conditions are unlikely to improve.

For the remaining 90% of claimants, the review recommends assessments that would be tailored to people’s individual circumstances. This would be a change from the current system which awards payments in four bands from £30.30 to £194.60 a week.

It said: “Those with the highest additional costs, and so the most significant needs, should receive the most support.” But it added: “This benefit is not appropriate for those who do not incur any additional costs associated with being disabled.”

The Resolution Foundation survey found one in six people – about 666,000 – say they currently claim Pip despite incurring no extra costs as a result of their disability. Ending payments for those people would save the government up to £4.4bn if applied in 2029/30, the thinktank said.
Officials say no final decisions have been made about how the assessments will work, or whether they will apply to existing claimants or only new ones.
If they are applied retrospectively, government sources say there are likely to be transitional arrangements to help people move on to the new system.
Andy Burnham has said he wants to bring the welfare bill down “as soon as possible”, though he has rejected what he says is the Conservative approach of imposing “crude cuts”.

Officials involved in drawing up the government’s response say the key question is how quickly to try to generate savings from the new system. One senior minister said: “The aim is still to bring the welfare bill down, the only question is how quickly.”
Even with Burnham’s more cautious approach, however, the prime minister risks a row with his backbenchers over the recommendations from both Milburn and Timms.

Debbie Abrahams, the Labour chair of the work and pensions committee, told the Commons on Tuesday: “We need to have extra support for disabled people to cover their extra costs, and that applies to everyone of all ages.”
The Labour MP Apsana Begum warned about “the deep anxiety that disabled people will have about reviews recommending changes to eligibility without having specifics provided”.
Related: The Guardian view on disability benefits: Timms’s radical review is rooted in experience | Editorial
Campaigners and charities welcomed Timms’ review, which was drawn up in consultation with disabled people, but urged the government not to leave vulnerable people without a financial lifeline.

Sarah Hughes, the chief executive of Mind, said: “It’s promising to see the recognition that Pip should be a cash benefit unless someone chooses other support in kind, that it is available to those in and out of work, and isn’t conditional on undertaking certain activities. However, in the wake of the Milburn review we know that many people – particularly those under 25 – are really worried that their lifeline will be cut.”

Svetlana Kotova, the director of campaigns and justice at Inclusion London, said: “It’s evident that when disabled people are actively involved in designing policy, the outputs better reflect the reality of our lives. Therefore, the government should prioritise the Timms recommendations over the reforms suggested by Milburn. The extra costs of disability do not start at 25.”
The Department for Work and Pensions said the new system would “help disabled people achieve better health, higher living standards and greater independence”.

articles.title: Israel attempts to jail Palestinian student at Hebrew University without trial
articles.summary: Mahdi Tounsi appeared to have suffered maltreatment at hearing where he was not allowed to hear prosecution case against him
body: Palestinian student Mahdi Tounsi appeared in a closed-door court hearing in Jerusalem, as academics and activists warned that Israel’s attempt to jail him without trial marked a serious escalation in attacks on Palestinian rights.
Yael Berda, a lawyer and sociology professor at Hebrew University, who has taught Tounsi for four years, came to court to call for his release.

“I have no doubt this is a case of political persecution based on identity and political activity,” she said outside the courtroom. “Mehdi’s arrest is part of a campaign that we’ve seen very much escalating since the elections.”
Her student was “almost unrecognisable” when he appeared on a video link in the courtroom, deprived of his glasses, with his hair and beard shaved and with visible bruising, she added.

Tounsi, a sociology and criminology student at Hebrew University in Jerusalem, was seized from his dorm on 8 November. He is held at Megiddo prison where documented abuse includes starvation rations, violent attacks on prisoners and rampant scabies and other diseases.

Thousands of Palestinians from the occupied West Bank are held under administrative detention orders but they have rarely been used against Palestinians who have Israeli citizenship or residence status in occupied East Jerusalem.
Prison authorities had not complied with a judge’s order to return Tounsi’s glasses, his brief public appearance on Tuesday showed.
Israeli prosecutors are seeking an administrative detention order, which allows for up to six months’ detention without trial or public presentation of evidence.
Security forces presented a summary of evidence in a hearing closed even to Tounsi and his lawyers, making a defence effectively impossible.

Tounsi’s arrest comes amid a racist campaign of delegitimisation against Palestinian citizens of Israel, whose votes were critical to stripping Benjamin Netanyahu’s coalition of its majority in elections last month.

Noa Dagoni, executive director of Jerusalem-focused rights group Ir Amin, described Tounsi’s arrest as a dangerous escalation in political persecution of activists, particularly those “at the junction of human rights, dialogue and non-violent action”.

Many of the Ir Amin staff count Tounsi as a personal friend after years working together in his home community of Silwan, where Israeli authorities are forcing mass displacements of Palestinians, including to make way for a theme park.

Dagoni fears he may have been targeted for this work. “We’re very concerned that this [arrest] has to do with his being a non-violent peace activist, also dealing with the displacement in his community,” she said.
“The partnership of Israelis and Palestinians is very intimidating for this government because it can be effective, it can build real political power.”
Officers from the Shin Bet security force failed to appear in court to present evidence at a first hearing last week, so the judge reconvened on Tuesday.

Reflecting concern about the case, his family and lawyer were joined in the courthouse by prominent activists, Knesset member Ofer Cassif, diplomats from Ireland, the Netherlands and the EU, his tutor and the dean of students from Hebrew University.
Hundreds of Jewish and Palestinian demonstrators gathered in the street outside calling for his immediate release.
Many knew Tounsi personally from classes or activism, including Lana, a Palestinian citizen of Israel.

“Someone who I know being kidnapped was really frightening,” she said. “It makes me think of my place here also, how it might affect me and if there are more people who I know who are going to be arrested soon.”

Many protesters were angry with university authorities, including Arielle, 27, a former student at the same campus. “Israeli universities need to take accountability for this, like they can’t allow students to be kidnapped from their dorm rooms,” she said.

Hebrew University’s dean of students, Zohar Kampf, said the university asked to testify but its request was rejected. The university has not commented on Tounsi’s violent arrest, deprivation of glasses and other mistreatment.

Cassif, the Knesset member, called for a global pressure campaign. “Where is the international community, especially academia. What are they waiting for?” he said. “Speak up, do something, raise your voice.”

The police did not respond to questions about visible marks of abuse or details of the case against Tounsi. A spokesperson said: “The suspect was lawfully arrested as part of an investigation conducted by the Jerusalem District Central Investigations Unit concerning ties to an act of terrorism.”

articles.title: More than 300 Russians killed as Moscow props up Mali’s junta, leaked data reveals
articles.summary: Exclusive: Records list 349 deaths in three years in Mali and also shed light on Russia’s military activity elsewhere in Africa
body: When the attack on Kidal began before dawn on 25 April this year, the Russian fighters were caught off guard. Within the first hour, checkpoints on the outskirts of the remote desert city nestled among the rocky hills of northern Mali had fallen to the insurgents, who pushed towards the police station where fierce fighting erupted.

“Everything was happening at once. Explosions were going off all around us, people were shouting,” recalled a former member of Russia’s Africa Corps who was stationed in Mali at the time and spoke on condition of anonymity. “Nobody knew where the enemy was coming from.”
Related: Russia’s war dead: the hidden toll of the Ukraine conflict

The Kremlin-controlled forces and their Malian allies were facing a coordinated surprise assault by the al-Qaida-linked JNIM and the Tuareg-led Azawad Liberation Front (FLA), whose fighters used suicide car bombs and drones to break through the city’s defences.

Leaked Russian state records suggest the losses were heavy that day. Death certificates of Russian fighters killed in Mali, held by Rosstat, Russia’s state statistics agency, were obtained by the hacker groups Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow and analysed by the Guardian.

The records show that 43 Russians died in Mali on 25 April, including six in Kidal and one in nearby Aguelhok. Others were recorded as dying in the capital, Bamako, and in Gao, where rebels shot down a Russian military helicopter that day.

By the following morning, the Russians had abandoned Kidal, which Russian mercenaries had helped capture in November 2023 and which Moscow had since held up as a showcase of its growing influence in Africa.
In all, the records list 349 Russian deaths in Mali between September 2023 and September 2026, most of which the Guardian was able to link to known battles with rebel groups.
The figures offer a previously unseen glimpse into the human cost of Moscow’s efforts to prop up Mali’s military junta, in what has become Russia’s largest military deployment in Africa.
Two western officials who have travelled to Mali and were shown the data said the death toll was higher than previously estimated.
“That’s over 10% of Russia’s forces killed in action,” said one of the officials, speaking on condition of anonymity because they were not authorised to comment publicly.
Related: Leaked data shows more than 1,000 Russian military suicides during Ukraine war
Moscow does not publish its losses in Africa, and its foreign ministry did not respond to a request for comment.

The Wagner private military group, led by the warlord Yevgeny Prigozhin, first arrived in Mali in late 2021, a year after a military coup had toppled President Ibrahim Boubacar Keïta. French forces were ordered to leave the country as relations with the junta deteriorated, bringing an end to France’s decade-long counter-terrorism operation and leaving Russia as the regime’s main foreign protector.

Wagner handed over its operations in Mali to the Africa Corps in June 2025, two years after Prigozhin led a failed mutiny on Moscow that discredited the group in the eyes of the Kremlin. By that summer, British intelligence estimated that about 2,000 Africa Corps personnel were deployed in the country.

The Africa Corps, closely overseen by Russian military intelligence, currently provides backing to several African governments in return for payment or lucrative contracts granting access to natural resources.

Despite the Russian presence, Mali’s security situation has continued to deteriorate. In late July 2024, Russian and Malian forces fought Tuareg separatists for several days near Tinzaouaten, on the Algerian border.
Wagner at the time issued a rare statement admitting losses, including the death of a commander, but gave no figure. Estimates from Russian sources ranged from about 20 to more than 80 dead.

The Rosstat records list 70 Russians who died on 27 July 2024, all but one of them in the Kidal region. The figures make the battle of Tinzaouaten the deadliest single day for Russian forces in Africa since Wagner mercenaries first deployed to the continent in 2017.

The toll in Mali may have been driven up by Ukraine, which has extended its war against Russia to the Sahel. Kyiv has been assisting Tuareg rebels there, according to two people with knowledge of the operations. CNN has reported that about 15 Ukrainian specialists were deployed to Mali to help local rebel forces fighting Russian troops.

The records are probably an undercount. Registration often lags, and no Russian deaths in Mali are recorded for March 2026 although at least three Africa Corps fighters were reported killed in an ambush near Nampala that month.

The leaked data also sheds light on Russia’s military activity elsewhere in Africa. Central African Republic, where Wagner fighters guard the president, Faustin-Archange Touadéra, accounts for 30 deaths. While not all could be linked to known incidents, three men died on the night drones struck Wagner camps in Kaga-Bandoro in December 2023.

In Libya, where Russian forces back the eastern commander Khalifa Haftar and use his airbases as a supply route to their deployments in the Sahel, some of the recorded deaths were probably linked to a helicopter crash at the Maaten al-Sarra base in February 2026. On Sunday, Ukrainian drones sunk a Russian warship off the coast of Libya; it is unclear whether there were any casualties.

In Niger, where Russia’s Africa Corps moved in after the military junta expelled French and US troops, a Russian fighter died two days after Islamic State militants attacked Niamey airport in January, a previously unreported casualty.

Moscow has in recent months stepped up its effort to show it is back in control in Mali. On 6 October, Malian troops and the Africa Corps recaptured Kidal after what the army called an air and ground campaign.

A report this month by the US-based Conflict Insights Group (CIG) found that the Africa Corps had sharply increased its use of drones in Mali, including Lancet suicide drones, amid an intensifying air campaign.

The group wrote that the drone campaign had also targeted civilians, boostering support for the rebels. “Civilian deaths in the intensified air campaign, which the Africa Corps leads, are likely to aid insurgent recruitment,” it said.
A western diplomat who works in the region said the attacks in late April had punctured the image of Russian military invincibility that Moscow and the junta had cultivated among Malians.
“Russia still wields considerable influence in Mali, but patience with its military performance is wearing thin.”

articles.title: What are the proposals for changing personal independence payment?
articles.summary: Review by social security minister Stephen Timms is designed to ‘rehumanise’ system. What will happen next?
body: A government-commissioned review has urged an overhaul of personal independence payment (Pip), a key disability benefit claimed by about 4 million people, with the aim of making it more humane and effective. How will it work and who will be affected?

The government on Tuesday published the Timms review of personal independence payment (Pip), a non-means-tested cash benefit not linked to employment status that helps about 4 million people in England, Wales and Northern Ireland meet the extra costs of disability or long-term illness (Scotland has adult disability payments). The Timms review emerged from the wreckage of the Labour government’s attempts to cut £5bn from Pip in 2025, which was brought down by public outrage and a backbench rebellion. Pip support – between £30.30 and £194.60 a week depending on need – is highly valued by claimants – but the assessment process has long been widely seen as dehumanising, capricious, and crude.

The review, which began a year ago, was to find ways to ensure Pip was fair, effective and fit for the future while helping disabled people to “achieve better health, higher living standards and greater independence” including through work. Co-chaired by the welfare minister, Stephen Timms, and the disability advocates Sharon Brennan and Clenton Farquharson, it was “co-produced” in consultation with tens of thousands of disabled people through surveys and workshops. A key part of its aim was to find ways of rebuilding public trust in Pip and the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP). It was not asked to look at the overall cost of Pip.

It confirms Pip is not fit for purpose and calls for a reformed disability benefit founded on the principles of dignity, choice and control. This would help disabled people to participate in society rather than focusing on what they cannot do. It would remain a non-means-tested, non-taxable, primarily cash benefit to people both in and out of work. It would “more closely reflect” real life needs, and the additional costs of disability and would run on a twin-track basis: people with serious conditions, or receiving end-of-life care, would qualify for speedy awards and would not have to submit to repeated eligibility reviews; others would undergo an “impact assessment”, which would “review how a person’s condition affects their daily life” to determine whether they would get a cash award. Those who are eligible for an award will have the option to choose services instead of, or as well as, cash, similar to the Motability car hire scheme.

Although Timms was not asked to look at Pip spending, or how to reduce it, his report is acutely aware of anxiety in government over the rising Pip bill, which rose from £14bn in 2019 to £25bn last year, and is forecast to rise to £34bn by the end of the decade (although Pip costs have risen, the overall working-age benefit bill as a percentage of GDP has remained stable for over a decade). While not proposing cuts, the review emphasises that a new system must more accurately reflect the “real life” extra costs of claimants. This suggests some claimants would no longer be eligible for cash support, others would receive less cash than currently, while others, with higher needs, might get a more generous award.

Unlike the Alan Milburn review, which proposed that disability benefits including Pip are scrapped almost entirely for 18- to 24-year-olds, saving £3.6bn a year by 2036, the Timms review does not recommend different, age-related benefit systems for disabled adults of working age. Many disability campaigners were taken by surprise by the Milburn recommendations, regarding them as a crude attempt to make savings, and worry that many young people would be pushed into acute hardship as a result.

Charities have broadly welcomed the Timms review. It is seen as laying the groundwork for a new system that is potentially fairer and more compassionate than the existing one, particularly for people with complex, degenerative or fluctuating conditions. But there is also widespread nervousness that changes will leave some vulnerable people without support – about half of Pip recipients are in material deprivation, and most food bank users have a disability. There are questions about how people’s “real life” additional costs will be identified and calculated, and how cash payments would work alongside services. A red line for campaigners is likely to be a guarantee that changes do not deepen hardship.

The government is expected to formally respond to both the Timms and Milburn reviews in the coming weeks before a formal white paper setting out policy plans in the new year. Ministers are expected to push ahead with changes to Pip but face a major decision over whether to adopt the Milburn recommendations, which could put it on a collision course with charities and backbenchers.

articles.title: Gaza issues meningitis epidemic alert after steep rise in cases
articles.summary: Health ministry records 272 new infections in October, more than eight times the normal monthly rate
body: Gaza’s health ministry has issued an epidemic alert after a sharp rise in meningitis infections, with more than 270 new cases reported in October.
Dr Nidal Ghoneim, a senior official at the ministry, said the spread of the disease posed a threat to the lives of hundreds of thousands of people, including children.

Health organisations attribute the rise in infections to the destruction of infrastructure, overcrowded shelters and the contamination of drinking water with sewage – a crisis made worse by winter flooding and restrictions on humanitarian aid. Much of Gaza’s drinking water previously came from desalination plants and three Israeli-controlled pipelines, which were cut off at the start of the war and have only partially reopened.

Ghoneim told a news conference that 272 meningitis infections had been reported in the territory in October, more than eight times the normal monthly rate of 30 to 50 cases. Fifteen Palestinians have died of meningitis since the beginning of this year, he said.

“We hold the [Israeli] occupation fully and directly responsible for the epidemic outbreak due to its prevention of the entry of maintenance spare parts, sterilisation materials and fuel,” the health ministry said.

The UN’s humanitarian agency (Ocha) had previously reported 413 suspected cases of meningitis in Gaza between 27 September and 31 October, including 294 viral and 119 bacterial cases. About 68% were recorded in Gaza City.
Ocha said the increase in cases could be attributed to crowded tents and schools, the deterioration of shelter and sanitation conditions and exposure to unsafe water.
Related: ‘We ​are tired from all this suffering’: displaced families in Gaza brace for another winter of misery
Gaza’s water crisis is severe. Before the war, 80% of the territory’s supply came from an aquifer that is now contaminated by seawater and wastewater, making it unfit for human consumption.

For many, this means a stark choice between drinking an extra cup of water or saving it to wash their hands and prevent disease. Acute diarrhoea is among the leading causes of illness in the territory. About 15,000 cubic metres a day of untreated waste seeps into the groundwater from soak-away pits, particularly in the informal camps in al-Mawasi.
The World Health Organization said in September that microbial contamination in water samples had risen from less than 6% in January to nearly 20% in August.

In addition to disease outbreaks and shortages of drinking water and basic necessities, Palestinians continue to face attacks and ceasefire violations by the Israeli military, which has intensified its strikes in recent days.

Soldiers crossed into Hamas-controlled central Gaza last Wednesday in the first ground operation across the “yellow line” boundary since a fragile ceasefire was agreed in October last year, forcing dozens of displaced Palestinians to flee their tents.
Four people were killed and seven wounded in Gaza over the past 24 hours, according to the health ministry, bringing the death toll since the ceasefire took effect to 1,679.
More than 74,000 Palestinians have been killed and more than 176,000 wounded since the beginning of the war in October 2023, according to Gaza’s health authorities.
